lessons.title: A secure development life cycle
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of a wheel with six colored spokes representing the stages of development, with a small shield at the center of the wheel.
objectives: Name the stages of a secure software development life cycle (secure SDLC).
Explain the value of addressing security as early as possible (shift left).
Carry out simple threat modeling with STRIDE.
Separate the development, test and production environments.

references.title: NIST SP 800-218, Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF)

blocks.text: Security at every stage

Secure software is not obtained by adding a test at the end. Security is built into every stage of the development cycle: from requirements to maintenance. The earlier a defect is found, the less it costs to fix.

blocks.title: The secure development life cycle
blocks.alt: Six-stage cycle around security: requirements, design, development, testing, deployment, maintenance, then back to requirements.

blocks.title: Shift left (décalage à gauche)
blocks.text: Practice of addressing security as early as possible in the development cycle (requirements, design, coding) rather than at the end. DevSecOps applies it by automating checks in the continuous integration and deployment pipeline.
A defect costs little on paper, more in the code, a lot in production: securing early means saving money.
Modeling threats
Threat modeling happens during design: you draw the application (data flows, trust boundaries), ask what can go wrong, then choose the controls. The STRIDE model helps you forget nothing.

blocks.title: Security requirements from the start
blocks.text: Security needs (authentication, logging, encryption, compliance) must be written alongside the functional needs. A requirement forgotten at the start becomes a design flaw, very costly to fix later.
Environments and changes

blocks.title: Organizational good practices
items: Separate development, test and production; developers have no write access to production.
Never use real production data in testing; use fictitious or anonymized data.
Send every release to production through change management (approval, planned rollback).
Have the code reviewed by another person before merging.
Remove debug accounts, comments and functions before going into production.

blocks.text: Exam questions often contrast "adding security at the end" with "building it in from the requirements". The right answer is almost always the earliest one. Also remember that separating environments is an application of separation of duties.

blocks.title: SOC case: a debug back door
blocks.text: On a simulated internal application, the analyst notices access to a "/debug" page that displays the server's variables, including a database password. The page had been added during development and never removed. The SOC triggers a password rotation, the team removes the page, and the pre-production checklist now includes a search for debug functions.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: Developer: threat modeling saves me from discovering flaws in production.
Architect: I draw the trust boundaries before writing the first line of code.
Auditor: I check that developers have no write access to production.
CISO: every project has security requirements approved before development starts.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: Security starts with requirements, not with testing.
STRIDE: each letter matches an attacked security property.
Production data in testing = potential leak.
A developer who deploys alone to production violates separation of duties.
Secure SDLC: requirements, design, development, testing, deployment, maintenance.
Shift left and DevSecOps: secure early and automate.
STRIDE: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, elevation of privilege.
Separate environments, fictitious data in testing, change management, code review.

lessons.title: Application flaws and the OWASP Top 10
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of a web form whose field contains an apostrophe and suspicious text, with a syringe stinging a database; next to it, a funnel-shaped filter holds back the suspicious text.
objectives: Name the main categories of the OWASP Top 10.
Explain SQL injection, XSS, CSRF and broken access control.
Choose the right countermeasure: parameterized queries, output encoding, anti-CSRF tokens, server-side checks.
Recognize buffer overflow and race conditions.

references.title: OWASP Top 10:2025 (top10.owasp.org/2025), with mapping to the 2021 edition

blocks.text: The OWASP Top 10

OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) is an open community that regularly publishes a list of the ten most critical risk categories for web applications. Here is the 2025 edition, with the mapping to the 2021 edition, still widely cited in training materials.

rows: Changing the ID in the URL to see someone else's account
Broadens A06 Vulnerable and Outdated Components
Unpatched library, malicious package, compromised pipeline
Sensitive data in cleartext, weak algorithms
No limit on the number of password reset attempts
Attack undetected for lack of logs or alerts
Unhandled error that opens access or reveals internal details

blocks.title: 2021 or 2025?
blocks.text: Many training materials still cite the 2021 edition. Remember both: in 2025, misconfiguration moves up to 2nd place, vulnerable components become the software supply chain (A03), SSRF joins access control (A01) and a new category appears for the handling of errors and exceptional cases (A10). Always read the year given in the question.
Injections

blocks.title: SQL injection (injection SQL)
blocks.text: Attack in which data entered by the user is interpreted as part of the SQL query, making it possible to read, modify or delete data. Main countermeasure: parameterized queries (prepared statements).

blocks.title: Cross-site scripting (XSS)
blocks.text: Injection of a script into a web page, which then runs in other users' browsers. It can be stored (saved on the server), reflected (sent back in the response) or DOM-based. Main countermeasure: output encoding of data, supplemented by a content security policy (CSP).

blocks.title: Four flaws, four countermeasures
blocks.alt: Four-cell table matching each flaw with its countermeasure: SQL injection and parameterized queries, XSS and output encoding, CSRF and anti-CSRF token, broken access control and server-side check on every request.

blocks.title: Validate on input, encode on output
blocks.text: Any data coming from outside is suspect. It is validated on the server side with an allow list (expected format, length, type), and encoded according to context when it is displayed. Validation in the browser improves convenience, but an attacker easily bypasses it.
SQL → parameterize. XSS → encode. CSRF → token. Access → check on the server side. "The client always lies".
Other flaws to know

rows: A malicious site makes a logged-in user's browser send a request
Anti-CSRF token, SameSite cookies, reauthentication for sensitive actions
Changing an identifier gives access to someone else's data
Check authorization on the server side for each object
Writing more data than the planned memory area, up to executing code
Length checks, memory-safe languages, system protections (ASLR, DEP)
The state changes between the check and the use
The server is led to call an address chosen by the attacker
Allow list of destinations, filtering of internal addresses

blocks.title: Mishandled errors (A10:2025)
blocks.text: An unexpected error can leave an operation half done, open access (fail open) or reveal details. An error that displays the SQL query, the server version or a stack trace gives the attacker a map of the application. In production, show the user a generic message and keep the details in the logs.
Exam classic: "what is the best defense against SQL injection?". The answer is the parameterized query. The WAF and input validation help, but they are not the main countermeasure.

blocks.title: SOC case: apostrophes in the logs
blocks.text: On an isolated demonstration application, the WAF logs requests containing "' OR 1=1 --" in the search field, then a response much larger than usual. The analyst concludes that an injection succeeded. The fix (parameterized query) is deployed, and the database access logs are used to measure the data exposed.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: Developer: I use parameterized queries and my framework's automatic encoding.
SOC analyst: a sudden rise in 500 errors on a form can signal an injection attempt.
Auditor: I check that access controls are done on the server side, not just in the interface.
CISO: the OWASP Top 10 serves as a minimum baseline for the security requirements of web projects.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: SQL injection → parameterized queries (not "escaping apostrophes by hand").
XSS → output encoding; the victim is the user's browser.
CSRF exploits the victim's already open session.
Client-side validation = convenience, never security.
Check the edition cited: A10 = SSRF in 2021, exceptional conditions in 2025.
OWASP Top 10:2025: access (with SSRF), configuration, supply chain, crypto, injection, design, authentication, integrity, logging and alerting, exceptional conditions.
SQL injection: parameterized queries. XSS: output encoding and CSP. CSRF: token.
Validate on the server side with an allow list; generic error messages.
Buffer overflow, TOCTOU, IDOR, SSRF: know how to recognize them.

lessons.title: Testing code and securing the software chain
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of a conveyor belt carrying boxes of code through three checkpoint gates marked analysis, tests and signature, up to a server.
objectives: Tell apart SAST, DAST, IAST, SCA and fuzzing.
Place automatic checks in a CI/CD pipeline.
Manage dependencies with a software bill of materials (SBOM).
Protect software integrity: code signing, secrets out of the code.

references.title: NIST SP 800-218, Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF)

blocks.text: The families of tests

rows: Reads the source code without running it
False positives; does not see the real configuration
Attacks the running application, from the outside
Does not show the line of code; late
Agent in the application during tests
Links the attack to the code
Inventories libraries and their known vulnerabilities
Does not see flaws in in-house code
Sends random or malformed data in bulk

blocks.text: SAST = read the code (white box, at rest). DAST = attack the application (black box, running).
A secure CI/CD pipeline

blocks.title: The automatic checks in the pipeline
blocks.alt: Five-step diagram: the developer pushes the code, static analysis and secret scanning run, dependency analysis produces the software bill of materials, dynamic analysis tests the application in pre-production, then the artifact is signed before deployment.

blocks.title: SBOM, software bill of materials (nomenclature logicielle)
blocks.text: Structured list of all the components of a piece of software (libraries, versions, suppliers). It tells you within minutes whether a newly published vulnerability affects your applications.

blocks.title: The software supply chain
blocks.text: A modern application is mostly made of code written by others. A vulnerable component, a malicious package or a compromised update affects everyone who uses it. You need to inventory (SBOM), monitor (SCA), choose reliable sources and verify signatures.
Integrity and secrets

blocks.title: Protecting the delivered software
items: Sign code and updates; verify the signature before installation.
Never write a password or a key in the code: use a secrets vault.
Automatically scan every commit for secrets; in case of a leak, revoke and replace the secret.
Protect the pipeline itself: accounts with MFA, minimal rights, logs.
Secure APIs: authentication, per-object authorization, rate limiting, input validation.

blocks.title: Code signing (signature du code)
blocks.text: Digital signature applied by the publisher to software or an update. It proves the origin (authenticity) and that the code has not been modified (integrity), but not that it is free of flaws.

Remember that no method is enough on its own: SAST and DAST are complementary, and manual penetration testing finds logic flaws that tools miss. In the exam, an answer that combines several methods is often the best.

blocks.title: SOC case: a key in the repository
blocks.text: The secret scanning tool flags a cloud access key in a commit pushed to a demonstration repository. Even if the commit is deleted, the key remains in the history: the SOC revokes it immediately, checks the cloud provider's logs to make sure it was not used, and the developer switches to the secrets vault.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: Developer: SAST results arrive in my merge request, and I fix them before merging.
SOC analyst: the SBOM tells me right away which applications are affected by a new CVE.
Auditor: I check that production deployments are signed and traced.
CISO: the pipeline is a critical asset: whoever controls it controls the delivered code.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: SAST = source code, without running it; DAST = running application.
A signature proves origin and integrity, not the absence of flaws.
Removing a secret from the code is not enough: it must be revoked.
SCA covers third-party components, not in-house code.
SAST, DAST, IAST, SCA, fuzzing, penetration testing: complementary methods.
CI/CD: automatic checks at every stage, protected pipeline.
SBOM and SCA to keep dependencies under control.
Code signing, secrets in a vault, API security.

questions.prompt: When should security work on a new piece of software begin?
choices: Just before it goes into production
As soon as the requirements are defined
After the first incident
During maintenance only
questions.explanation: Security requirements are written along with the functional requirements: that is when fixing costs the least.

whyNot.0: Too late: design flaws are then expensive.
whyNot.2: Reacting after an incident is not a secure development approach.
whyNot.3: Maintenance comes at the end of the cycle.

questions.prompt: In STRIDE, what does the letter E stand for?
choices: Exposure (of data)
Elevation of privilege
Encryption bypass
Exfiltration (data theft)
questions.explanation: STRIDE: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege.

whyNot.0: It is not a letter of the model.
whyNot.2: Encryption is a control, not a STRIDE threat.
whyNot.3: Exfiltration falls under information disclosure (I).

questions.prompt: Which practice is recommended for testing an application?
choices: Giving the testers the customers' passwords
Using fictitious or anonymized data
Copying the production database as is
Testing directly in production
questions.explanation: Test environments are less protected: real data does not belong there.

whyNot.0: There is no legitimate reason for this; it is a leak.
whyNot.2: Real data in test creates a risk of leakage.
whyNot.3: Testing in production endangers the service and the data.

questions.prompt: A user denies having approved a wire transfer and no log can prove otherwise. Which STRIDE threat was not addressed?
choices: Denial of service
Tampering
Spoofing
Repudiation
questions.explanation: Repudiation is addressed with protected logs and signatures that prove who did what.

whyNot.0: The service is not interrupted.
whyNot.1: The data is not modified.
whyNot.2: Spoofing concerns the identity of the sender, not the proof of their action.

questions.prompt: What does "shift left" mean in secure development?
choices: Addressing security as early as possible in the development cycle
Postponing security testing until the end of the project
Handing all security over to the operations team
Moving the servers to the left of the architecture diagram
questions.explanation: Security activities (requirements, design, coding, automated tests) are moved earlier to find defects early.

whyNot.1: That is the opposite.
whyNot.2: Security becomes everyone's business, from the start.
whyNot.3: A play on words with no connection.

questions.prompt: A developer can modify the code and deploy it to production alone, without approval. Which principle is violated?
choices: Defense in depth only
Open design
Fail safe
Separation of duties
questions.explanation: Writing and deploying without another person's review makes it possible to introduce an error or a backdoor without detection.

whyNot.0: The principle directly violated is separation of duties.
whyNot.1: Open design concerns the secrecy of the design.
whyNot.2: Fail safe concerns failures.

questions.prompt: When is threat modeling most useful?
choices: At disposal
During the annual audit
After going into production
During design
questions.explanation: It is used to choose controls before writing the code; it is updated as the application evolves.

whyNot.0: Too late to influence the design.
whyNot.1: The audit checks; it does not design.
whyNot.2: It can be revised, but its main value is at design time.

questions.prompt: An urgent fix must go into production that same evening. What is the right approach?
choices: Follow the emergency change procedure, with a rollback planned
Wait for the next monthly change board meeting, no matter what
Let each developer decide alone whether to deploy it tonight
Deploy it directly, with no ticket or record, to go faster
questions.explanation: Urgency speeds up the process but does not remove it: traceability and rollback remain mandatory.

whyNot.1: Waiting can leave an exploitable flaw.
whyNot.2: No oversight, no separation of duties.
whyNot.3: An unrecorded change is a major risk.

questions.prompt: Which checks should be made before putting an application into production? (several answers)
choices: Removing debug pages and accounts
Checking that secrets are not in the code
Disabling detailed error messages for users
Leaving the test credentials for support
questions.explanation: Debug features, verbose errors and secrets in the code are classic go-live flaws.

whyNot.3: Test credentials in production are an entry point.

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of a code review by another person?
choices: Checking the spelling and layout of the code comments
Finding flaws the author missed, with a second pair of eyes
Slowing projects down to give the tests time to finish
Replacing all automated tests with a human check
questions.explanation: A second pair of eyes spots defects and makes it harder to deliberately introduce malicious code.

whyNot.0: That is not the main goal.
whyNot.2: That is not the goal.
whyNot.3: It complements the tests; it does not replace them.

questions.prompt: What is the best defense against SQL injection?
choices: Disk encryption
Hiding error messages
Parameterized (prepared) queries
A long password for the database
questions.explanation: With a parameterized query, the input remains data and is never interpreted as SQL.

whyNot.0: Disk encryption changes nothing about the query.
whyNot.1: Useful, but injection remains possible.
whyNot.3: The injection goes through the application, which is already connected.

questions.prompt: In an XSS attack, where does the malicious code run?
choices: In the backup system, during a restore
In the browsers of the users who view the page
In the application firewall placed in front of the site
On the database server that stores the page
questions.explanation: The injected script runs in the victims' browsers, for example to steal their session.

whyNot.0: Unrelated.
whyNot.2: The firewall does not run the script.
whyNot.3: That is the case of SQL injection.

questions.prompt: What does OWASP publish with its "Top 10"?
choices: A mandatory certification standard for websites
The most critical categories of web risks
The ten network ports to close first on a web server
The ten best antivirus products on the market, tested every year
questions.explanation: The Top 10 is an awareness document, updated regularly (latest edition: 2025), used as a minimum baseline.

whyNot.0: It is not a mandatory standard.
whyNot.2: It is not a list of ports.
whyNot.3: It is not a product comparison.

questions.prompt: By changing "invoice=1001" to "invoice=1002" in the URL, a customer sees someone else's invoice. Which category is this?
choices: Cryptographic failure
Denial of service
SSRF
Broken access control
questions.explanation: The application does not check that the requested object belongs to the user: this is an IDOR, a case of broken access control.

whyNot.0: The problem is not encryption.
whyNot.1: The service works.
whyNot.2: The server does not call another address.

questions.prompt: A user logged in to their bank visits a booby-trapped site that triggers a transfer without their knowledge. Which countermeasure protects best?
choices: Encrypting the customer accounts database
A session-specific anti-CSRF token in each sensitive form
An up-to-date antivirus installed on the bank's server
A longer password for the user's account
questions.explanation: The booby-trapped site does not know the token: the forged request is rejected. SameSite cookies add further protection.

whyNot.0: Encryption does not single out a forged request.
whyNot.2: The request looks legitimate to the server.
whyNot.3: The session is already open.

questions.prompt: Why is input validation in the browser not enough?
choices: Because modern browsers prohibit it
Because it is too slow for large forms
Because an attacker can bypass it and call the server directly
Because it encrypts the data, which the server can then no longer read
questions.explanation: The client is under the user's control: security validation is always done on the server side.

whyNot.0: It is allowed and useful for convenience.
whyNot.1: Speed is not the problem.
whyNot.3: It encrypts nothing.

questions.prompt: Which main countermeasure prevents stored XSS in a site's comments?
choices: A daily backup of the comments database
TLS encryption of every page of the site
Context-aware output encoding of the data at display time
Network address translation (NAT) in front of the web server
questions.explanation: Once encoded, the script is displayed as text instead of running. A CSP also limits which scripts are allowed.

whyNot.0: The backup also keeps the script.
whyNot.1: TLS protects the transport, not the displayed content.
whyNot.3: Unrelated.

questions.prompt: Which measures reduce the risk of buffer overflow? (several answers)
choices: Using memory-safe languages when possible
Showing memory addresses in error messages
Checking the length of the data being copied
Enabling system protections such as ASLR and DEP
questions.explanation: Length checks, safe languages and system protections make exploitation much harder.

whyNot.1: Showing addresses actually helps the attacker.

questions.prompt: A program checks that a file belongs to the user, then opens it a few milliseconds later; in the meantime, an attacker replaces it with a link to a system file. What type of flaw is this?
choices: Request forgery (CSRF)
SQL injection (SQLi)
Race condition (TOCTOU)
Cross-site scripting (XSS)
questions.explanation: Time of check to time of use: the state changes between the check and the use. Countermeasure: atomic operations and locks.

whyNot.0: There is no cross-site request.
whyNot.1: There is no SQL query.
whyNot.3: There is no web page.

questions.prompt: An "import an image from a URL" feature makes it possible to have the server call the address of an internal administration service. Which countermeasure is the most appropriate?
choices: An up-to-date antivirus on the administrators' workstations
Restricting destinations and blocking internal addresses
Hiding the SSID of the administration Wi-Fi network
A longer password for the users' accounts
questions.explanation: Against SSRF, you restrict the destinations the server can reach and filter internal addresses. In the OWASP Top 10:2025, SSRF is folded into A01 (access control); it was A10 in 2021.

whyNot.0: The problem is on the server side.
whyNot.2: Unrelated to Wi-Fi.
whyNot.3: No effect on what the server calls.

questions.prompt: Which method analyzes the source code without running the application?
choices: Load testing
SAST
Fuzzing
DAST
questions.explanation: Static analysis (SAST) reads the code and flags risky lines.

whyNot.0: Load testing measures performance.
whyNot.2: Fuzzing runs the program with malformed data.
whyNot.3: DAST tests the running application.

questions.prompt: What does the digital signature of an update prove?
choices: Its origin and the fact that it has not been modified
That it is free of charge
That it contains no flaws
That it is compatible with every system
questions.explanation: The signature guarantees authenticity and integrity, not the quality of the code.

whyNot.1: Unrelated.
whyNot.2: A vendor can sign vulnerable code.
whyNot.3: Unrelated.

questions.prompt: Where should the database password used by an application be stored?
choices: In a code comment, for the developers
In cleartext in the source code, in a constant
In a secrets vault, read at startup
In the repository name, so it is easy to find
questions.explanation: The secrets vault protects and logs secrets, and allows them to be rotated without changing the code.

whyNot.0: Same problem.
whyNot.1: Anyone who reads the repository sees the secret.
whyNot.3: Absurd and visible.

questions.prompt: A critical vulnerability is published in a very widely used library. Which tool quickly shows which applications use it?
choices: The SBOM (software bill of materials) of each application
The business continuity plan of each application
The developers' password policy
The data center visitor log
questions.explanation: The SBOM lists the components and their versions: you search for the library and get the list of affected applications.

whyNot.1: It does not list software components.
whyNot.2: Unrelated.
whyNot.3: Unrelated.

questions.prompt: What advantage does DAST have over SAST?
choices: It never produces false positives, because it exploits the flaw
It shows exactly which line of code is at fault
It observes the real behavior of the deployed application, with its configuration
It can run even before the code is written
questions.explanation: DAST tests the running application from the outside: it sees configuration and runtime problems.

whyNot.0: No tool is free of false positives.
whyNot.1: That is the advantage of SAST.
whyNot.3: It needs a working application.

questions.prompt: An API key was pushed to a shared repository by mistake. What is the first action?
choices: Delete the commit from the repository and do nothing else
Wait to see whether anyone uses the key before acting
Rename the repository so the key is harder to find
Revoke the key and issue a new one, then check whether it was used
questions.explanation: The key remains in the history and may have been copied: only revocation makes it unusable.

whyNot.0: The history and copies keep the key.
whyNot.1: Waiting lets the attacker act.
whyNot.2: The repository name changes nothing.

questions.prompt: What does software composition analysis (SCA) do?
choices: It measures the application's speed under heavy load
It replaces code review with an automated check
It encrypts the source code before publication
It inventories third-party components and their known flaws
questions.explanation: SCA relies on known vulnerability databases for the libraries in use.

whyNot.0: Unrelated.
whyNot.1: It does not look at in-house code.
whyNot.2: It encrypts nothing.

questions.prompt: An attacker compromises a vendor's build server and inserts malicious code into a signed update. What lesson should be drawn?
choices: The build pipeline must be protected, in addition to the signature
The problem comes from the users, who should have checked the installed code
The signature is always enough: a signed update is necessarily safe
All software updates should be stopped to avoid this type of attack
questions.explanation: If the compromise happens before signing, the signature authenticates trojanized code: the whole chain must be protected.

whyNot.1: The users could not have detected it.
whyNot.2: The signature proves the origin, not that the code is clean.
whyNot.3: No longer patching creates other risks.

questions.prompt: Which testing program best covers a critical web application?
choices: No testing: a well-tuned web application firewall (WAF) is enough to block everything
DAST alone, run directly on the production environment
Continuous SAST and SCA, DAST in preproduction, manual penetration test
SAST alone, run once a year before the compliance audit
questions.explanation: The methods complement one another: continuous automation and a human eye on business logic.

whyNot.0: The WAF is one layer, not a substitute for secure code.
whyNot.1: Late and partial.
whyNot.3: Too infrequent and too partial.

questions.prompt: Which measures protect an API exposed on the Internet? (several answers)
choices: Rate limiting
An API key written into the public mobile app
Validation of the data received
Authentication and authorization for each requested object
questions.explanation: Authenticating, authorizing object by object, rate limiting and validating input are the basics.

whyNot.1: A key embedded in a public app can be extracted by anyone.
